coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: Consumer Protection (Scrap Metal) Regulations 2019 (Government Notice 2019): licence for dealers/exporters (annual fee Rs 15,000 per 2016 amendment, 35% surcharge on late renewal), carrier permit Rs 5,000, collector permits for employees (badge). Dealers keep a received-metal register (description, weight, date/time, seller name, NIC number, address, sum paid, vehicle number) and a dispatch register, kept 5 years and open to inspection; carriers keep a register in the vehicle. Candidate C1.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: No Mauritian pawnbroker or general second-hand licensing source found. Second-hand jewellery trade-in is regulated under the Jewellery Act 2007 and the Jewellery (Dealer's Registration and Transactions) Regulations 2012 (see C2).

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Jewellery Act 2007 Part IV; Regulations 2012: dealer registration valid up to 3 years, 25% surcharge on late renewal, trade-in records (declaration of ownership, ID, receipt) kept 5 years on premises, trade-in form with a 10-day holding period, transactions only on registered premises. Candidate C2, related to K02 (AML duty differs).

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: Nothing found. No Mauritian end-of-life-vehicle or dismantler licensing source surfaced; results were other countries. Only a 1999 import measure allowing used motor parts. Unverified whether any register exists.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: One combined search found no Mauritian register for livestock traders or animal transport. Meat Act and National Agricultural Products Regulations 2013 (NAPRO) cover slaughter only. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Slaughterhouse licence from NAPRO (Ministry of Agro-Industry), reported fee Rs 1,000 a year, valid one year (wiki source only). Meat Act 1990 licences meat premises. Tiny buyer group; weak candidate C10.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: Nothing found for Mauritius in the one combined search; no beekeeper register or rule surfaced.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: Veterinary Council Act 2020 (Act 12 of 2020): registration, annual list/register, annual fee, CPD. Veterinary medicines fall under the Pharmacy Act 1983. Very few buyers (vets); weak candidate C9.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Ground Water Act 1969 and Ground Water Regulations 2011: licence from the Central Water Authority, meter and daily abstraction records, monthly charges. Water Resources Act 2024 (Act 9 of 2024, Gazette 25 July 2024): water use permits, borehole drilling provisions (Part IV), registration of existing water rights (Part V), transitional section 81. Commencement and deadline not confirmed. Candidate C3.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: Local Government (Dumping and Waste Carriers) Regulations 2021 (waste carrier licence) and Waste Water (Registration of Waste Water Carriers and Disposal of Waste Water) Regulations 2006 (registration with the Waste Water Management Authority). Record or reporting duties not seen. Candidate C6.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: No Mauritian legal text found in the search. Apave Mauritius sells statutory inspection of pressure equipment and lifting equipment, so periodic inspection exists. Candidate C8 is unverified.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: No search spent; budget used on other categories. Only indirect: Central Water Authority is the main supplier, so private small water systems are unlikely.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Use of Pesticides Act 2018 (Pesticides Regulatory Office under the agriculture ministry) and Chemical Fertilizers Control Act (premises licence, separate storage from food). coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Private Recruitment Agencies Act 2023 (proclaimed Feb 2024 per press) and Private Recruitment Agencies Regulations 2025 (Council of Ministers 19 Sept 2025): type-specific licences, fit-and-proper screen, repatriation duty backed by a security deposit, regular inspections; a minister reportedly cited a Rs 1 million guarantee (June 2026). Penalty Rs 500,000 to 1 million and up to 5 years. 2026 proposal: employers must show local recruitment (Employment Information Centre certificate) before foreign hires. Candidates C4 and C5.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: Nothing found. Search returned no Mauritian source; no verified licence or register for funeral directors.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Registration of Associations Act 1978 (Act 35): notify formation in 14 days, register in 3 months, annual return under section 23 (content and deadline not seen); Ministry of Labour, Registrar of Associations. Candidate C11. Halal/kosher: not searched.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: NLTA licensing commission and disciplinary committee to be reorganised and online taxi platforms regulated (June 2026 press); a Fleet Management System for real-time tracking announced (2025); electric bus transition costing operators. No fleet-age or filing rule found. Candidate C12.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Money changers and forex dealers are licensed by the Bank of Mauritius under the Banking Act 2004; 2007 call set capital of Rs 3 million and online data submission to the Bank. No hawker licence rule found. Candidate C13 (small group).

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: ECCEA (Early Childhood Care and Education Authority, 2007 Act) runs registration and re-registration of pre-schools and childminders; daycare accreditation by the Child Care Accreditation Bureau. No Mauritian tattoo or driving-school licence rules found (driving licences are issued by Police Traffic Branch). Candidate C14. Small food producers and hunting not searched.

coverage.category: 21. Fuel stations and fuel or LPG distributors
coverage.found: Market is state-controlled: the State Trading Corporation imports fuel and LPG, pump prices are set by the state, and LPG is distributed by two firms (Vivo/Shell, Total) plus a new entrant (allAfrica Sept 2026). No small-operator register or recurring report found. Petroleum Act licence categories unconfirmed (the one hit was not shown to be Mauritian). Nothing new.

coverage.category: 22. Grain, coffee, cocoa and other commodity traders, millers and warehouses
coverage.found: Sugar sector is regulated by the Mauritius Cane Industry Authority Act 2011. Small planters (under 10 ha) are tied to the Sugar Insurance Fund Board and a 2025 transport-cost refund regulation (GN 60 of 2025). Only importers, millers and refiners selling sugar locally must register with the Authority. No recurring filing for small firms found; low software pull.

coverage.category: 23. Co-operatives, credit unions and savings groups
coverage.found: Co-operatives Act 2016 provides for an auditor licensed under section 73 and an AGM each financial year. No current Registrar filing rules, deadlines or e-portal found. Unverified.

coverage.category: 24. Private clinics, labs and other health providers that bill insurers or state schemes
coverage.found: Private Health Institutions Act 1989: annual permit of Rs 5,000-25,000 from the Ministry of Health's Permanent Secretary; section 9(g) lets the Permanent Secretary request tariff documents. Competition Commission market inquiry into private medical care opened April 2026, with conclusions expected October 2026 and possible legislation on billing transparency. Insurer-claim workflows not checked.

coverage.category: 25. Pharmacies, medicine importers, and users of controlled chemicals or precursors
coverage.found: Pharmacy Council Act 2015 (registration of pharmacists, CPD regulations 2018) and Pharmacy Act 1983. No current renewal procedure, controlled-drugs register rules or 2025 changes found. Unverified.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: Private security companies are licensed by the Commissioner of Police (Private Security Section); fee figures on community wiki pages conflict (Rs 1,000 vs Rs 10,000). Workers' Rights Act amendments (Finance Act 2024) make labour contractor and hirer jointly liable for migrant workers' pay, safety and contributions. Cleaning agencies: no regime found. See candidate on foreign-worker employers.

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: Registration and renewal now sits with the Construction Industry Authority (successor to the CIDB under the CIDB Act 2008). A law-firm article claims the 2025/26 Budget revised grading thresholds and renewal deadlines; unconfirmed. Official site not reached.

coverage.category: 28. Notaries, land agents, real estate brokers and other professionals with periodic or anti-money-laundering reports
coverage.found: Notaries and real-estate agents are reporting persons under FIAMLA and must register on FIU goAML (FIU notice of 27 March 2024; new licensees must register within 5 working days). Administrative penalty regulations took effect 18 November 2025; a 2026 AML/CFT/CPF reform (Act 3 of 2026, in force 18 April 2026) is reported. Same buyer and duty as K02, so no new candidate.

coverage.category: 29. Hotels, guest houses and short-term rentals: guest registers, tourism levies
coverage.found: MRA tourist fee of EUR 3 per tourist per night from 1 October 2025; all tourist accommodation managers must register with the MRA. Only about 10% of an estimated 5,000+ rental units reportedly hold a Tourism Authority licence (secondary source). Same as K01. Guest-register rules not found.

coverage.category: 30. Small exporters and importers facing traceability or certification rules: food, fish, timber, forest-risk commodities
coverage.found: Fish export regulations: exporters register with Veterinary Services and need an export health certificate for each consignment (2009 regulations; current status unconfirmed). Singapore Food Agency notice (14 July 2026) says Mauritius requires an EHC on all imported seafood from 1 December 2026, a foreign-exporter duty, not a Mauritian buyer.

coverage.category: 31. Data protection: controller registration and records of processing (Data Protection Act 2017)
coverage.found: The Data Protection Office communique of 20 Feb 2025 says all organisations, professionals and sole traders (doctors, lawyers, notaries, jewellers, bookmakers) must register as controllers. Registration is valid 3 years, with renewal due within 3 months before expiry; fees Rs 1,000 / 1,500 / 2,500 by headcount (2020 regulations, may be outdated). Section 33 requires a record of processing operations. Penalty: up to Rs 200,000 or 5 years.

coverage.category: 32. Liquor licences (Excise Act 1994, MRA)
coverage.found: MRA issues and renews retail (off, on-and-off) and wholesale liquor licences each year. Renewals after 14 January 2026 carry a 50% surcharge; fees were changed by the Finance Act 2025; a Rs 1,500 processing fee has applied to new and transferred licences since 1 October 2025. Payment is online or by direct debit. A free MRA channel already covers renewal.

coverage.category: 33. Employers of foreign workers: lodging permits, work and occupation permits, recruitment certificates
coverage.found: 3,059 employers held a valid Lodging Accommodation Permit at 31 July 2025 (OSH Employees' Lodging Accommodation Regulations 2011). OSH (Centralised Lodging Accommodation) Regulations 2026 approved June 2026. Employers will need an Employment Information Centre certificate before foreign recruitment. Permit applications or renewals are refused unless at least 90% of workers with expired permits were regularised. Migrant-worker liability framework added to the Workers' Rights Act in 2024. Six agencies are licensed to recruit foreign workers (valid to 2029; Rs 1m guarantee).

coverage.category: 34. Gambling: bookmakers, totalisator and racing licences (Gambling Regulatory Authority)
coverage.found: Finance Act 2026 (Act 14 of 2026, assent 12 Aug 2026) amends the GRA Act. Licence fees move to a calendar-year basis (changes from 1 July 2027). Bookmakers may run up to 5 terminals, which must be registered with the MRA and connected to CEMS. Racing-season licence applications and renewals are due to the GRA by 30 Nov 2026. Few operators, so a niche.

coverage.category: 35. Local-authority trade licences and food premises (Local Government Act 2011, Food Act 1998)
coverage.found: Trade fees have been paid to the Corporate and Business Registration Department since January 2020; only occasional-activity and advertising fees (GN 252 of 2019) are still paid to the council. No Mauritian food-premises registration procedure found. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 36. Registered associations (Registration of Associations Act 1978)
coverage.found: Section 23 requires an annual return to the Registrar of Associations. Deadline, content and filing channel not found. Unverified.

coverage.category: 37. Fisheries Act 2023: fishers, fishmongers, vessels and gear registers

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: Mauritius has no real small private water-system sector. CWA produces, treats and distributes drinking water, and CWA labs sample daily (AllAfrica interview, June 2026, per search snippet). The only private-side duty found is groundwater abstraction. Under the Ground Water Act 1969 and Ground Water Regulations 2011 (GN 240/2011), a licence is needed to abstract. It runs up to 7 years and is non-transferable, with a written application in the Second Schedule form. The Water Resources Act No. 9 of 2024 (Gazette 25 July 2024) adds water-use permits (Part III) and borehole regulation (Part IV), with a Water Resources Commission to keep a permit register. This was only partly confirmed: I did not verify commencement or renewal rules, and the UNEP/LEAP page and AllAfrica pages returned HTTP 403 on fetch. A February 2025 AllAfrica snippet says there are about 600 boreholes nationally, a third owned by CWA, and that illegal or expired-permit operators are being pursued. That leaves roughly 400 private permit holders, which is too few to sell to. Drinks producers once had to file monthly metered-water returns under the CWA (Production of Drinks) Regulations 2011. Those were revoked in 2013 (GN 74/2013), and I found no successor. Bottled water falls under Food Regulations 1999 reg. 421 and the Environment Protection (Drinking Water Standards) Regulations 1996; not checked whether these are still in force. I found no private tanker or water-vendor licensing regime: the only tanker news was an internal CWA probe of its own drivers selling water illegally (Feb 2025). Nothing new beyond K01/K03 and nothing sellable in this category.

result.competitor: I found no software, app or online state portal for Mauritian borehole permits or abstraction returns. The only known provider is the drilling and hydrogeology consultancy Geocrust Ltd, reported by the discovery pass and not re-checked here. Not checked: whether a govmu e-licensing route exists.
result.duty: The Water Resources Act 2024 (Act 9 of 2024, assent and Gazette No. 77, 25 July 2024) requires water use permits, permit payments, and borehole drilling and use controls, and provides for registration of existing water rights. Commencement (s.82), the transitional rules (s.81), registration deadlines and penalties were not reached: the PDF text could not be extracted and the LEAP page returned 403. The earlier Ground Water Regulations 2011 required an application to the CWA, an approved meter at the abstraction point and monthly returns and charges. Whether these were superseded is unverified. A February 2025 enforcement case under the old regime involved an expired borehole permit, and the CWA anti-fraud section and police acted. The Water Resources Commission was publishing reservoir data in 2026, which suggests it is operating, but this does not prove the Act is in force.
result.market: No register count found. Press (fr.allafrica.com, February 2025) says private boreholes exist across the island, owned by farmers, industrialists and other approved applicants. The discovery pass reported about 600 boreholes from a snippet; I did not verify this. In February 2025 about 174 boreholes were being tested or drilled, mostly by the state. The likely market is a few hundred private permit holders at most.
result.reason: I confirmed the Water Resources Act 2024 exists: Act 9 of 2024, Gazette No. 77 of 25 July 2024. It sets up water use permits (s.21-27, including payment for the permit), boreholes (s.44-47) and registration of existing water rights. I could not find a proclamation of commencement, the text of transitional s.81, or a deadline. The 2011 Ground Water Regulations required metered abstraction and monthly returns, so there is some recurring duty, but it is unclear whether those rules still stand. I found no software or online portal, but the market is small: press mentions private boreholes owned by farmers and industrialists, with no register count. Most of the work is a one-off permit or registration, best handled by a consultant. Low frequency and few buyers.

result.competitor: I found no dedicated software or state portal for this licensing work in my searches, but competitor checking was limited (no dedicated competitor query). The likely substitutes are lawyers and consultants handling the one-off licence application.
result.duty: Private Recruitment Agencies Act 2023 (proclaimed Feb 2024) plus Private Recruitment Agencies Regulations 2025 (in force Oct 2025). A Ministry of Labour licence is needed for each type of recruitment: local, Mauritians abroad, or foreign workers into Mauritius. New companies must post a Rs 1m guarantee and show capitalisation, a business plan, 3 years of financial statements, proof of recruitment experience and a legal representative. Penalty for recruiting without a licence: Rs 500,000 to 1m and up to 5 years in prison. Licences are valid until 2029, so the main duty is a multi-year application rather than a recurring filing. Recurring returns, inspections and register duties were not confirmed because the Gazette text was not found.
result.market: 20 licensed agencies as of June 2026, per the Minister of Labour as reported by L'Express via AllAfrica: 10 local-to-local, 4 placing Mauritians abroad, 6 bringing foreign workers into Mauritius. The total number of applicants is unknown but probably small, from a few dozen up to perhaps 100.
result.reason: The duty is real. The Private Recruitment Agencies Act 2023 was proclaimed in February 2024, and its 2025 Regulations took effect in October 2025. Agencies need a separate licence for each recruitment type, a Rs 1m guarantee for new companies, a business plan, 3 years of accounts and proof of experience. Recruiting without a licence carries a fine of Rs 500k to 1m and up to 5 years in prison. No competitor was found, but I ran only a light check. The market is tiny: the minister reported 20 licences in June 2026 (10 local, 4 placing Mauritians abroad, 6 bringing foreign workers in). Licences run until 2029, so renewal is rare. I did not confirm any recurring returns or a placement register because I could not find the Gazette text. Buyers are likely to use lawyers or consultants for the one-off application. There is too little frequency and too few buyers to support a product.

result.competitor: The core steps run through free state systems: the E-Work Permit platform/NELS (applications and tracking), the Mauritius Job Platform (job listings and candidate search) and the EIC certificate. EDB runs a free G2G digital recruitment platform with India's NSDC. Licensed foreign-labour recruitment agencies (six authorised, 20 agency permits issued since October 2025) and work-permit consultants do the paperwork as a service. No private software found for tracking local-recruitment evidence, but search depth was limited.
result.duty: Proposed, not confirmed as in force. On 25 June 2026 (allAfrica/l'express) Labour Minister Reza Uteem described a recommendation from an interministerial committee. Employers would have to prove they tried to recruit locally by publishing the job offer and consulting local databases, including the Mauritius Job Platform. An Employment Information Centre certificate "sera nécessaire" (future tense) before any request to recruit abroad. No Gazette notice or start date was found by October 2026. Already in force: work permit applications have long needed proof of advertising in two newspapers (secondary source, undated). New or renewal permits are refused if fewer than 90% of workers with expired permits have been regularised. The penalty for the proposed rule is not specified, and the minister said the law must change before the ministry can impose administrative sanctions. Government Notice 129 of 2026, under the Workers' Rights Act, is in force but targets fictitious associations and co-operatives, not local recruitment.
result.market: As of 31 May 2026, 51,945 foreign workers held a valid work permit or exemption certificate: 23,249 in manufacturing and 15,542 in construction. From June 2025 to March 2026 there were 41,833 work permit applications. The number of employers was not found and is probably low thousands, heavily concentrated in larger manufacturers and construction firms.
result.reason: The duty is still only proposed. In June 2026 Minister Uteem described a recommendation from an interministerial committee: employers would advertise, consult the Mauritius Job Platform and get an Employment Information Centre certificate. No Gazette text or start date was found as of October 2026. Workers are 51,945, but the number of employers is unknown. The work is tied to free state systems (the E-Work Permit portal, NELS, the Job Platform, the EIC). Licensed recruitment agencies already handle the paperwork. That leaves a thin layer for evidence tracking, with low frequency and a small market. GN 129/2026 is about fictitious associations, not this duty.

The duty is real. The Consumer Protection (Scrap Metal) Regulations 2019 (GN 151/2019) have applied since 16 Sept 2019. They require a licence from the Permanent Secretary, with a yearly fee of Rs 15,000 per the 2016 amendment and a 35% late surcharge. The MRA notice requires customs registration for exporters. Searches found no software, state portal or public register doing the job. I did not search in French. I did not find the number of licensed dealers, so the market is probably tens to low hundreds of firms. That is a tiny, informal, low-tech buyer base with weak willingness to pay and no clear distribution channel. Whether the 2019 text still includes the exporter category after the 2016 amendment is unclear. Low score for market size.

The duty is real, but I only saw the ICNL copy of the 1978 Act, so any later amendment is unchecked. Under s.23(1) the secretary must file an annual return within 3 months of the accounting date. It contains the certified AGM statement, officer names and addresses, the membership count and any amended rules. Officer changes must be reported within 14 days (s.23(2)). The AGM is required under s.22. Penalty under s.37 is a fine of up to Rs 500 and/or up to 3 months in prison, which is trivial. Searches found no software or online portal for associations. I found no association count. Willingness to pay is low (volunteer secretaries, low penalty, a simple form), so the score is 3.

result.duty: Jewellery Act 2007 and Jewellery (Dealer's Registration and Transactions) Regulations 2012: dealer registration (up to 3 years, renewable) and records and receipts
result.market: not_reached: no public count of registered dealers found
result.reason: Duty is real: Jewellery Act 2007 (in force 9 May 2008, bar ss.21 and 25) Part IV, plus Dealer's Registration and Transactions Regulations 2012. These cover dealer registration valid up to 3 years, and records and receipts. The 2012 regulations are amended (GN 9 of 2012). I did not re-verify the 5-year retention, the 10-day holding period or the 25% surcharge, and I found no 2025-26 amendments. No software or free state tool for Mauritian dealers appeared in two searches. The market is tiny and I found no public dealer count. The Assay Office has no public register, so the buyer list is hard to reach. Enforcement frequency is unknown. Low willingness to pay, so the idea is only viable as a K02 add-on.

I could not confirm the legal basis. Four searches found no Mauritian text on lift, boiler, pressure-vessel or lifting-gear examination: no regulation name, interval, penalty or authority. Third-party summaries (Rivermate) only name the OSH Act 2005, and none of its listed regulations covers this equipment. The Apave Mauritius page confirms it sells regulatory inspections of pressure and lifting equipment, but it cites no law, interval or software, and does not mention lifts. I found no local tracker software and no owner count. The duty is plausible but unproven. Inspections are done by third-party inspectors, so the owners' pain is mainly scheduling, and the market is small. A solo founder would likely have to sell through the inspectors.

Duty is real: Data Protection Act 2017 requires controller registration, valid 3 years, renewal within 3 months before expiry. Failure is an offence (fine up to Rs 200,000 or 5 years). Section 33 requires a record of processing. Fees come from the Data Protection (Fees) Regulations 2020. No Mauritius-specific SME software turned up. Only generic frameworks (theartofservice, consentstack, clym) and local consultants (e.g. rogerscapital.mu) appeared. Weaknesses: the DPO already runs an online registration portal, so the core filing is free to do; renewal comes once per 3 years; fees are low. Market size is not quantified, and the local-language search was not done. The fee table was not retrieved. Low revenue per customer and a thin recurring workflow keep the score at 3.

result.reason: Only one source supports the claim, a commercial law-firm blog that mixes the names CIA, CIDB and CIAM. It gives no renewal period, fees, penalties or section numbers. I could not reach any official Mauritian source (CIDB site, Laws of Mauritius, Gazette), and search results were mostly South Africa and Sri Lanka. The duty is plausible, since the CIDB Act 2008 does register and grade contractors. The renewal cycle and penalty are unconfirmed, and registration looks like a one-off or periodic renewal per firm, not a frequent workflow. Competitors were not found, and I could not check them directly. The market is probably a few thousand contractors. Willingness to pay looks low and the workflow is thin (a reminder tracker). Keep the score at 3.
